newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Towering inferno kills 32 in HK shopping district.
newsitem.headline: Towering inferno kills 32 in HK shopping district.

text.p: Fire swept through a 16-floor shop and office block in a bustling Hong Kong tourist district, killing more than 30 people and injuring scores in the territory's worst high-rise building blaze.
The inferno flared up on Wednesday evening and raged through the night, gutting seven floors. More than 200 firemen were still battling the fire 17 hours later on Thursday morning.

People trapped behind sealed windows on Wednesday ripped off burning clothes, while others scrambled to safety. A plume of flame lit up the sky above the famed Hong Kong harbour but later gave way to a black cloud of smoke.
The death toll climbed as rescue work continued in the Garley Building on Nathan Road, the "golden mile" of the Kowloon peninsula tourist district.

The government said 32 people were known to have died, including a fireman, and police said up to 10 people were still believed to be missing. Officials said 17 of the charred bodies were found on the 15th floor on Thursday morning.

In February 1992, 26 people were killed and 126 injured in a blaze at a Vietnamese refugee camp in Shek Kong in the rural New Territories, and in January 1994, 12 staff were killed by a fire at a Hong Kong bank branch in Shek Kip Mei.
Six people died in a fire in a slum hostel in the Shamshuipo district of Kowloon in December 1990.
Hong Kong's worst fire on record was in 1918 when 600 people were killed and 400 injured in a blaze at the Happy Valley Race course on Hong Kong Island.
As the search for bodies continued, officials sounded alarm bells about building safety, an issue of long-running debate in the densely populated British colony.
"Since the old building does not have modern fire protection facilities, rescue operation is particularly difficult," fire chief Peter Cheung told reporters. An inquiry was launched.

Governor Chris Patten visited the spot and said the tragedy intensified the need to tighten safety regulations to help to prevent such fires. Many of Hong Kong's older buildings have very few anti-fire devices, if any at all.
In dramatic scenes, firefighters plucked more than 90 survivors from the block, a maze of small offices, shops and workshops, and some were winched off the blazing roof by helicopter.
The fire broke out early on Wednesday evening and rapidly engulfed the first four storeys of the building.
It then raced up the elevator shaft and swept through the top three floors, deputy fire chief K.Y Tsang said.
The smoke blanked out the vision of helicopter pilots who flew dangerous missions over rooftops to winch up survivors.
Others jumped from window ledges on to rescue ladders and some scrambled on to air conditioners, watched helplessly by friends and relatives far below in the crowded street.
One of the dead was a fireman killed while battling the blaze. Liu Chi-ho, 40, plunged down a lift shaft.

Another man fell from the building in a rush to escape. Witnesses said they saw him climb from a window and cling to an air conditioner. It gave way and sent the man tumbling several storeys on to a canopy, where he lay crumpled and still.
